docs.title: Operating Model
docs.text: Version: 2.0 Status: Current State (Phase 1) with Future State (Phase 2) Roadmap Platform: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Primary Language: R Region: europe-west2 (London) Source Control: GitHub

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The NDAP Research and Development Directorate (RDD) Application Platform provides a standardised Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) framework for the development, testing, deployment and execution of R-based analytical workloads on Google Cloud Platform (GCP).

The platform enables analytical teams to focus on developing business logic and statistical methodology whilst deployment, runtime orchestration and infrastructure management are increasingly standardised and automated.

The current Phase 1 implementation provides:

  • Standardised GitHub repository structures
  • Automated CI/CD pipelines
  • Controlled promotion through Development and Production environments
  • Reproducible R environments through renv
  • Automated deployment using GitHub Actions
  • Runtime execution through Vertex AI Workbench
  • Configuration-driven deployments
  • Shared reusable deployment workflows

The future Phase 2 evolution transitions the platform towards a centrally managed Platform Engineering model built around:

  • Containerisation
  • Artifact Registry
  • Cloud Run Jobs
  • Cloud Scheduler
  • Workload Identity Federation
  • Golden runtime images
  • Thin application repositories

This transition will significantly reduce operational overhead, minimise platform drift, improve scalability and reduce infrastructure costs through a fully serverless, pay-per-use architecture.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
Multiple RDD teams develop and operate analytical products that transform, process and publish public health data.

Historically, analytical applications have required bespoke deployment approaches, operational processes and runtime environments. This creates challenges around:

  • Consistency
  • Reproducibility
  • Supportability
  • Security
  • Cost optimisation

The NDAP RDD CI/CD Platform addresses these challenges through the introduction of a common deployment architecture that can be reused across all analytical teams.

Examples include:

  • RDD PHOF
  • RDD PCC
  • RDD SHRN
  • Future RDD analytical teams

docs.title: Architecture Objectives
docs.text:
The platform has been designed to achieve the following objectives.

Standardisation

Enable all RDD teams to follow a common deployment pattern.

Automation

Eliminate manual deployment activities wherever possible.

Security

Provide controlled access, environment segregation and secure deployment pathways.

Reproducibility

Ensure analytical code executes consistently between environments.

Scalability

Allow new teams to onboard without creating new infrastructure patterns.

Cost Efficiency

Reduce operational costs through shared architecture and reusable tooling.

Maintainability

Centralise common functionality and minimise duplicated engineering effort.

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
Principle 1 — Everything is Version Controlled

All application code, workflow definitions and deployment artefacts originate from Git repositories.

Principle 2 — Production Must Be Earned

Every deployment must progress through controlled promotion stages before reaching Production.

Principle 3 — Automate Everything Possible

Deployments, validation steps and runtime provisioning should be automated wherever practical.

Principle 4 — Shared Components Belong to the Platform

Common deployment functionality should be centrally maintained rather than duplicated across repositories.

Principle 5 — Runtime Environments Must Be Reproducible

Applications should execute using deterministic runtime configurations.

Principle 6 — Isolation Reduces Risk

Workloads should be separated wherever possible to minimise blast radius.

docs.title: Regional Deployment
docs.text: All environments are deployed within: GCP Region europe-west2(London)

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: GCP projects are divided in two planes: Application & Data, which are further divided into two environments: Development & Production

docs.title: Application Projects
docs.text:
ndr-tr-phw-app-dev (Development)

ndr-tr-phw-app-prod (Production)

Responsibilities include:

  • Deployment artefacts
  • Runtime execution
  • Vertex AI infrastructure
  • Application orchestration

docs.title: Data Projects
docs.text:
ndr-tr-phw-dp-dev (Development)

ndr-tr-phw-dp-prod (Production)

Responsibilities include:

  • Dataset storage
  • Table management
  • Data processing
  • Analytical outputs

docs.title: Benefits of Segregation b/w application & data
docs.text:
Reduced Blast Radius

Compromise or failure of application services does not automatically compromise data storage environments.

Improved Security

Different IAM policies may be applied to application and data layers.

Operational Isolation

Application changes can occur independently of data platform changes.

Governance

Improves auditing and ownership of platform components.

docs.title: Repository Naming Convention
docs.text:
Repositories follow a common naming convention.

ndap-app-rdd-repo or team name

Examples:

ndap-app-rdd-phof

ndap-app-rdd-pcc

ndap-app-rdd-shrn

This enables consistency and discoverability across the platform.

docs.title: Branching Strategy
docs.text:
The platform follows a simple promotion model.

feature/* | v dev | v main

docs.title: Feature Branch
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Development
  • Bug fixes
  • Enhancements
  • Refactoring

Examples:

feature/new-indicator feature/refactor-processing feature/bug-fix

docs.title: Development Branch
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • Integration testing
  • System testing
  • End-to-end validation

Deployment Target:

ndr-tr-phw-app-dev

docs.title: Main Branch
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • Production releases

Deployment Target:

ndr-tr-phw-app-prod

docs.title: Pull Request Governance
docs.text: Pull Requests are mandatory for branch promotion.

docs.title: Feature → Dev
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Peer review
  • Pull Request approval
  • Successful deployment
  • Validation of outputs

docs.title: Dev → Main
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Peer review
  • Pull Request approval
  • Successful development validation
  • Release acceptance

docs.title: Development Lifecycle
docs.text:
Step 1 – Build

Analysts develop R code using:

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Google Cloud SDK
  • Development GCP resources

Step 2 – Commit

Changes are committed into a feature branch.

Step 3 – Review

Pull Request raised into Dev branch.

Step 4 – Deploy to Development

CI/CD pipeline automatically deploys the solution.

Step 5 – Validate

Outputs are reviewed and validated.

Validation approaches vary by team:

  • Full E2E runs
  • Workflow dispatch controlled runs
  • Targeted validation activities

Step 6 – Promote to Production

Changes are promoted through a Pull Request into Main.

Step 7 – Deploy to Production

Automated deployment executes against Production resources.

docs.title: CI/CD Process Diagram
docs.text: The CI/CD framework consists of:

docs.title: Application Repository
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Business logic
  • R code
  • Configuration
  • Package requirements

docs.title: Shared Platform Repository
docs.text:
Repository:

Public-Health-Wales/ndap-rdd-app-reusable-cicd

Owns:

  • Deployment logic
  • Runtime orchestration
  • Common CI/CD activities

This prevents duplication across analytical teams.

docs.title: deploy.yml
docs.text:
Acts as the orchestration layer.

Capabilities:

  • Automated deployment
  • Workflow dispatch
  • Environment selection
  • Secret management
  • Reusable workflow invocation

docs.title: Environment Selection
docs.text:
main -> Production

all other deployment branches -> Development

docs.title: Secret Selection
docs.text: Environment-specific GitHub Secrets are automatically passed to the shared deployment workflow.

docs.title: Shared Deployment Workflow
docs.text:
Repository:

ndap-rdd-app-reusable-cicd

Workflow:

reusable-deploy.yml

docs.title: Sequence of Events
docs.text: Validate Inputs | Authenticate | Package Artefacts | Upload Artefacts | Stop Vertex Instance | Update Metadata | Restart Vertex Instance | Trigger Runtime

docs.title: Runtime Execution Sequence (File Level)
docs.text:
Execution begins after the Vertex instance starts.

Vertex Startup | v setup.sh | v run_R_script.sh | v Target R Script

docs.title: setup.sh Responsibilities
docs.text:
The startup script performs infrastructure validation.

Responsibilities:

  • Configure environment variables
  • Initialise logging
  • Validate artefact checksums
  • Verify package existence
  • Launch execution pipeline

Calls:

bash run_R_script.sh

docs.title: run_R_script.sh Responsibilities
docs.text:
Responsible for runtime control.

Functions include:

  • Environment verification
  • renv activation
  • Lock file management
  • R script invocation

docs.title: generate_lock.sh Responsibilities
docs.text:
Responsible for dependency management.

Activities:

  • Verify Conda environment
  • Create environment if missing
  • Install dependencies from packages.txt
  • Generate renv.lock

This guarantees reproducible package versions.

docs.title: Sensitive Configuration
docs.text:
Stored in: GitHub Secrets

Examples:

  • Service account credentials
  • Authentication secrets

docs.title: Non-Sensitive Configuration
docs.text:
Stored within GCS-hosted configuration files.

Examples:

  • Dataset names
  • Table names
  • Bucket names
  • Project names

Benefits:

  • Environment portability
  • Reduced code changes
  • Easier operational management

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
Mandatory Peer Review:

Required at:

Feature -> Dev Dev -> Main

Environment Isolation:

Development and Production operate independently.

Credential Segregation:

Each environment uses dedicated credentials.

Controlled Deployment Path:

Production deployments must originate from approved source-controlled changes.

Project Segregation:

Application and data projects remain logically separated.

docs.title: Multi-Team Operating Model
docs.text:
The architecture is intentionally replicated across RDD teams.

Benefits:

  • Consistent platform experience
  • Reduced support complexity
  • Standard onboarding process
  • Shared operational tooling

docs.title: Current State Assessment (Phase 1)
docs.text:
The current architecture successfully delivers:

  • Automated deployments
  • Reproducible execution
  • Shared deployment workflows
  • Controlled environment promotion
  • Reusable CI/CD capabilities

However, several challenges remain.

Increased Duplication & Complexity:

Nearly all the scripts in CI/CD process are replicated in each team's deployment pipeline, resulting in significant duplication, complexity and forcing analysts/scientists to undertake engineering maintenance activities.

Infrastructure Cost:

Vertex AI Workbench incurs standing infrastructure costs even when workloads are not running.

Runtime Management Complexity:

Workbench lifecycle management introduces operational overhead.

Shared Runtime Risks:

Multiple workloads can execute on a shared runtime environment.

This increases potential blast radius.

docs.title: Target State Architecture (Phase 2)
docs.text: The strategic direction for the platform is a move towards a Platform Engineering operating model.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
Analytical teams should focus exclusively on:

  • Business logic
  • Statistical methodology
  • Data transformation

The platform should own:

  • Runtime management
  • Container builds
  • Deployment orchestration
  • Dependency management
  • Security controls

docs.title: Phase 2 Platform Model
docs.text:
Refer to NDAP Proposed Architecture

Thin Repository:

Application repositories will contain only:

Application Code workflow.yml packages.txt Configuration

All deployment logic will reside centrally.

Benefits:

  • Plug-and-play onboarding
  • Minimal duplication
  • Simplified maintenance
  • Consistent standards

Golden Runtime Images:

The platform will maintain approved base images.

Examples:

R 4.4 Base Image R 4.5 Base Image

These images will include:

  • Approved R versions
  • Approved package baselines
  • Common platform tooling

Stored within:

Artifact Registry

Benefits:

  • Zero Runtime Drift: Development and Production execute identical images.
  • Consistent Package Versions: Eliminates environment inconsistencies.
  • Faster Deployments: Common packages no longer require installation during execution.
  • Simplified Support: One known runtime baseline.

docs.title: Cloud Run Execution Model
docs.text:
Phase 2 replaces long-lived runtime infrastructure with ephemeral execution.

Container Starts | Execute Workload | Container Stops

Benefits:

  • Pay-Per-Use: Only pay when workloads execute.
  • No Standing Charges: No idle infrastructure costs.
  • Better Cost Efficiency: Ideal for scheduled analytical workloads.
  • Automatic Scaling: Supports platform growth without infrastructure redesign.

docs.title: Share-Nothing Architecture
docs.text:
Each workload executes independently.

Workload A | Container A

Workload B | Container B

Workload C | Container C

Benefits:

  • Minimal Blast Radius: Failure impacts only the affected workload.
  • Improved Reliability: No shared runtime contamination.
  • Better Isolation: Applications execute independently.
  • Predictable Behaviour: Every run starts from a clean environment.

docs.title: Immutable Deployments
docs.text:
Container images become versioned deployment artefacts.

Benefits:

  • Improved auditability
  • Easier rollback
  • Predictable releases

docs.title: Strategic Outcome
docs.text:
Phase 1 standardised how analytical applications are deployed.

Phase 2 standardises the platform itself.

The future operating model removes infrastructure concerns from analytical teams and provides a centrally managed, reusable and cost-efficient platform.

Analysts focus solely on analytical code.

The platform provides:

  • Deployment
  • Security
  • Runtime management
  • Dependency management
  • Monitoring
  • Scaling
  • Governance

This results in a modern, cloud-native analytical platform that is easier to operate, cheaper to run, faster to scale and significantly more resilient than the current state.

docs.title: NDAP R Common: For the Users, By the Users
Overview
docs.text:
NDAP R Common is a community-driven repository of reusable R functions, utilities, and code components designed to be shared across Public Health Wales (PHW) and the wider NHS Wales community.

The initiative follows a simple principle:

Write once, use many times.

Instead of multiple teams independently developing similar functions, common solutions can be developed collaboratively, stored centrally, and reused across projects, directorates, and organisations.

This approach helps reduce duplication, improve consistency, accelerate delivery, and foster a stronger data and analytics community.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
To create a shared ecosystem of reusable R code where analysts, data scientists, and developers contribute and consume common functions in the same way they use an R package.

The goal is to:

  • Break down organisational silos
  • Encourage collaboration
  • Promote code reuse
  • Improve quality through peer contribution
  • Reduce development effort across teams
  • Establish common standards and approaches

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text:
NDAP R Common operates as a central Git repository that acts as a library of reusable functions and code modules.

Contributors from across PHW can publish common functionality that has value beyond a single project.

Examples include:

  • Data cleaning functions
  • Validation routines
  • NHS Wales lookup functions
  • Statistical utilities
  • Reporting helpers
  • Visualisation templates
  • Data quality checks
  • Geospatial functions
  • API connectors
  • Common ETL components

Once published, other teams can call these functions directly without needing to rewrite them.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text:
Users and teams contribute reusable code into the R Common repository.

Examples:

  • RDD analytical teams
  • CDSC teams
  • Other PHW directorates
  • Platform engineering teams
  • NHS Wales partner organisations

Each contribution is reviewed and incorporated into the shared library.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
Functions are stored in a structured Git repository with:

  • Documentation
  • Version control
  • Coding standards
  • Example usage
  • Testing where applicable

This ensures contributions remain reliable and maintainable.

docs.title: Consume
docs.text:
Users can access and utilise shared functions just as they would any other R package.

For analysts, the experience is familiar:

library(ndaprcommon)

clean_nhs_postcode(data)
validate_welsh_lhb(code)
generate_standard_report(dataset)

Consumers focus on solving business problems rather than rebuilding common functionality.

docs.title: Breaking the Silo Mentality
docs.text:
Historically, many teams solve the same problems independently:

  • Multiple postcode cleaning functions
  • Multiple validation scripts
  • Multiple report-generation routines
  • Multiple implementations of identical business logic

This results in:

  • Duplicate effort
  • Inconsistent outputs
  • Higher maintenance costs
  • Limited visibility of good work

NDAP R Common changes this model by creating a shared platform where innovations developed by one team can benefit everyone.

One team's solution becomes everyone's asset.

docs.title: Accelerated Delivery
docs.text: Teams can leverage existing solutions instead of starting from scratch.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
• Faster project delivery
  • Reduced development effort
  • Increased productivity

docs.title: Improved Quality
docs.text:
Shared functions are:

  • Reviewed
  • Reused
  • Tested by multiple teams

This naturally improves code quality and reliability.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
• Fewer defects
  • Better maintainability
  • Greater confidence in analytical outputs

docs.title: Consistency Across PHW
docs.text:
Common functions lead to common approaches.

Examples:

  • Standardised calculations
  • Consistent data cleansing
  • Shared validation logic
  • Unified reporting methods

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Different teams produce consistent and comparable outputs.

docs.title: Knowledge Sharing
docs.text: The repository becomes a living catalogue of analytical expertise.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
• Reduced knowledge silos
  • Wider adoption of best practices
  • Increased cross-directorate collaboration

docs.title: Community-Led Innovation
docs.text:
The repository is developed for the users, by the users.

Contributors are not limited to a central development team.

Every analyst, developer, and data scientist can contribute improvements and new capabilities.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The platform continuously evolves based on real user needs.

docs.title: PHW and NHS Wales Collaboration
docs.text: While initially focused on Public Health Wales, the model can extend beyond departmental boundaries.

docs.title: Public Health Wales
docs.text:
Contributions and consumption can come from:

  • RDD
  • CDSC
  • Screening Programmes
  • Corporate Services
  • Other Directorates

docs.title: Wider NHS Wales
docs.text:
The shared repository can also support:

  • Health Boards
  • NHS Trusts
  • National Programmes
  • Partner Organisations

This creates opportunities for broader collaboration and standardisation across Wales.

docs.title: Governance Principles
docs.text: To ensure sustainability, contributions should adhere to agreed standards.

docs.title: Code Standards
docs.text:
• Documented functions
  • Clear naming conventions
  • Reusable design
  • Peer-reviewed changes

docs.title: Quality Assurance
docs.text:
• Testing where appropriate
  • Version-controlled releases
  • Change history
  • Backward compatibility considerations

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
While governance provides oversight, ownership remains community-driven.

The success of NDAP R Common depends on active participation from its users.

docs.title: Expected Outcomes
docs.text:
By adopting NDAP R Common, Public Health Wales can:

  • Eliminate unnecessary duplication of effort
  • Accelerate analytics development
  • Improve code quality and consistency
  • Foster a culture of collaboration
  • Share expertise across organisational boundaries
  • Establish reusable analytics building blocks
  • Create a sustainable community of practice

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
NDAP R Common is more than a code repository—it is a collaborative framework for knowledge sharing and reusable analytics development.

By enabling teams to contribute and consume common R functions through a shared repository, the platform promotes standardisation, reduces duplicated effort, and helps build a connected analytics community across Public Health Wales and NHS Wales.

For the Users, By the Users.

Share once. Reuse everywhere. Reinvent nothing.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The NDAP (National Data Analytics Platform) architecture is designed as a cloud-native, automated, and governed analytics platform built on Google Cloud Platform (GCP). The architecture emphasizes Infrastructure as Code (IaC), DevOps automation, secure data management, and self-service analytics through modern reporting tools.

The proposed high level architecture of NDAP is pictured below:

docs.title: Platform Layers
docs.text:
The platform is organized into four logical layers:

  1. Development Layer
  2. Integration Layer
  3. Security & Observability Layer
  4. Google Cloud Platform Runtime Environment

docs.title: Development Layer
docs.text: The Development Layer provides the foundation for collaborative software development, infrastructure management, and analytics enablement.

docs.title: Source Code Repository
docs.text:
The platform source code is maintained using:

  • GitHub
  • Visual Studio Code (VS Code)

This repository contains:

  • Data pipeline code
  • Infrastructure-as-Code definitions
  • Deployment configurations
  • Scheduling definitions
  • Analytics application code

docs.title: Consumer Analytics Layer
docs.text:
Business users consume analytical outputs through:

  • Microsoft Power BI
  • R
  • Shiny Applications

These tools provide dashboards, reports, and advanced analytical capabilities based on data processed within the NDAP platform.

docs.title: Key Benefits
docs.text:
• Version-controlled development
  • Collaborative engineering workflows
  • Automated deployment pipelines
  • Traceability and auditability
  • Support for both analysts and technical users

docs.title: Integration Layer
docs.text: The Integration Layer automates platform provisioning, application deployment, and operational workflows.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: This layer is made up of the below components:

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text: GitHub Actions serves as the Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) engine.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Code validation
  • Automated testing
  • Build automation
  • Deployment orchestration
  • Artifact publishing

When developers commit changes to GitHub, GitHub Actions automatically initiates deployment workflows.

docs.title: Terraform
docs.text: Terraform is used as the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) framework.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Provision GCP infrastructure
  • Manage cloud resources
  • Maintain infrastructure consistency
  • Enable repeatable deployments

Terraform definitions are stored alongside source code and executed through GitHub Actions pipelines.

docs.title: Artifact Registry
docs.text: Artifact Registry acts as the central repository for deployment artifacts.

docs.title: Stored Assets
docs.text:
• Container images
  • Runtime packages
  • Application artefacts

Artifacts produced during CI/CD processes are published here before deployment into runtime services.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Version control of deployable assets
  • Secure package management
  • Controlled promotion across environments

docs.title: Security & Observability Layer
docs.text: The Security & Observability Layer provides governance, compliance, and operational controls across the platform.

docs.title: Security & Access Policies
docs.text:
Security policies define:

  • Role-based access control (RBAC)
  • Principle of least privilege
  • Data access controls
  • Environment segregation
  • Compliance requirements

These policies govern both user activities and service-to-service interactions.

docs.title: Data & Coding Standards
docs.text: The platform operates under established standards covering:

docs.title: Data Standards
docs.text:
• Data modelling
  • Metadata management
  • Data quality
  • Naming conventions
  • Lifecycle management

docs.title: Development Standards
docs.text:
• Code quality
  • Testing requirements
  • DevOps practices
  • Documentation standards

These standards ensure platform consistency, maintainability, and regulatory compliance.

docs.title: Google Cloud Platform Environment
docs.text: The runtime environment hosts all operational components of the NDAP platform within Google Cloud.

docs.title: Run Layer
docs.text: The Run Layer contains services responsible for executing workloads.

docs.title: Cloud Scheduler
docs.text:
Cloud Scheduler provides:

  • Scheduled execution of pipelines
  • Time-based orchestration
  • Automated workflow triggering

Typical use cases include:

  • Daily data ingestion
  • Periodic reporting refreshes
  • Scheduled analytical processing

docs.title: Cloud Run
docs.text:
Cloud Run hosts containerized services that perform:

  • Data processing
  • APIs
  • Scheduled workloads
  • Business logic execution

Applications are deployed from images stored in Artifact Registry.

docs.title: Data Layer
docs.text: The Data Layer provides storage, analytics, and governance capabilities.

docs.title: BigQuery
docs.text: BigQuery serves as the primary analytical data warehouse.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Data storage
  • Data transformation
  • Advanced analytics
  • Reporting datasets
  • Query execution

docs.title: Cloud Storage
docs.text: Cloud Storage provides scalable object storage.

docs.title: Typical Usage
docs.text:
• Raw data landing zones
  • File-based ingestion
  • Intermediate processing outputs
  • Archival datasets

docs.title: Dataplex
docs.text: Dataplex provides data governance and metadata management across the platform.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Data discovery
  • Governance
  • Metadata management
  • Data quality oversight
  • Data domain organisation

Together, these services form a governed enterprise data platform.

docs.title: Security Layer
docs.text: The Security Layer secures platform operations and supports monitoring.

docs.title: IAM & PAM
docs.text:
Identity and Access Management (IAM) and Privileged Access Management (PAM) provide:

  • User authentication
  • Service account management
  • Access governance
  • Privileged access control

docs.title: Cloud Logging
docs.text: Cloud Logging provides centralized observability.

docs.title: Captured Information
docs.text:
• Application logs
  • Infrastructure logs
  • Audit logs
  • Security events
  • Operational telemetry

This enables monitoring, troubleshooting, incident response, and compliance reporting.

docs.title: End-to-End Workflow
docs.text:
The typical platform workflow operates as follows:

  1. Developers create or update code in GitHub using VS Code.
  2. GitHub Actions automatically executes CI/CD pipelines.
  3. Terraform provisions or updates cloud infrastructure.
  4. Build artefacts are published to Artifact Registry.
  5. Cloud Run workloads are deployed from the registered artefacts.
  6. Cloud Scheduler triggers workloads according to defined schedules.
  7. Data is ingested and processed within Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
  8. Dataplex governs datasets and metadata across the data estate.
  9. IAM and PAM enforce security and access controls.
  10. Cloud Logging captures operational and audit information.
  11. Curated datasets are consumed through Power BI, R, and Shiny dashboards for analytics and reporting.

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
The NDAP architecture is built around the following principles:

  • Cloud-native design using managed GCP services.
  • Infrastructure as Code through Terraform.
  • DevSecOps automation with GitHub Actions.
  • Centralized governance using Dataplex and organisational policies.
  • Secure-by-design access controls via IAM and PAM.
  • Scalable analytics using BigQuery.
  • Reusable containerized workloads running on Cloud Run.
  • Comprehensive observability through Cloud Logging.
  • Business self-service analytics via Power BI, R, and Shiny.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The NDAP Platform Architecture establishes a secure, scalable, and automated data analytics ecosystem on Google Cloud. The platform combines modern DevOps practices, governed data management, cloud-native compute services, and enterprise-grade security controls to support the full lifecycle of data ingestion, transformation, analytics, and reporting.

docs.title: Introduction to Working in GCP
docs.text: This page provides a starter guide to setup and connect to GCP from your local system. Since GCP is a remote system, you have to connect to it using a Google provided gateway and authenticate yourself. Please follow the steps below to do that.

docs.title: Project Access
docs.text:
1. Ensure you have GCP access. Please drop a mail to Service Desk requesting access. Line manager approval is needed.
  2. Once done, please connect with NDAP Data Engineering team to be added to appropriate GCP projects and GCS buckets.
  3. Projects you will need access to: Please discuss with your team colleagues. If you are unsure, please reach out to NDAP Data Engineering team. Generally, there are four projects:
  4. Ndr-tr-phw-dp-dev: This is the development area project which contains data i.e. tables and files
  5. Ndr-tr-phw-dp-prod: This is the production area project with data.
  6. Ndr-tr-phw-app-dev: This is the development area project which contains all applications. Your codes will run here.
  7. Ndr-tr-phw-app-prod: This is the production area project which contains all applications. Your production live codes will run here.
  8. Please check if you have access to the projects by clicking on the links below:
  9. dp-dev
  10. dp-prod
  11. app-dev
  12. app-prod

docs.title: Data Access
docs.text: Access to GCP projects may not always give you access to data. Data access is often restricted as per usage requirements so you may need to request for additional access to buckets and tables.

docs.text:
1. Check you have access to the right project buckets on Google Cloud Storage. Ensure you are in dp-dev project (or prod) and then navigate to GCS Buckets
  1. You should be able to see a list like below:
  1. Click on your team bucket and see if you can see contents. For example, if you click on rdd-dp-dev bucket and you should see more folders:
  1. Do the same check for app-dev in GCS:
  1. If you get any error message at any point, please reach out to NDAP Data Engineering team.

docs.title: Table Access
docs.text:
1. Check you have access to the right BigQuery DataSets. Ensure you are in dp-dev project (or prod) and then navigate to BigQuery
  1. Click on the triangle-type symbol on the middle pane and then expand the ndr-tr-phw-dp-dev:
  2. You should be able to see a list like below:
  1. Click on your team Dataset and see if you can see list of tables. For example, if you click on rdd-dev-ind dataset, you should be able to see tables under if, if you have access.

docs.title: Working in GitHub
docs.text: GitHub is a version control service, that maintains your artefacts (code, documents etc) in remote locations (called repositories). These repositories are access controlled to maintain security. It allows you to work in your local, make changes, and sync the changes to the remote repository through secure connections. It maintains version of artefacts (we will call it codes for easy understanding) through something called branches. You can think of branches as snapshots of entire codebase.

docs.title: Branching Model in NDAP
docs.text:
In PHW-NDAP, we follow a thre branch model:

  • Every repository usually have multiple feature branches. When you want to make any changes, you would want to take a copy of the latest code in your own area (which is called feature branch), make changes, do unit tests, and once done, sync the feature branch changes to remote repo (push the code).

  • Next up: Dev branch. Think of it as the place where everyone's changes are merging together, but you still need to check if the whole thing is working before marking it as the final version. So, you raise a request to merge your feature branch to dev branch (this is called a Pull request). This request is usually peer reviewed and then merged. Usually, we do a round of overall testing to ensure everything is in order.

  • Finally, a main branch, which is the golden production version of code. Since this is the cleanest and best version of code, making changes to this branch is restricted, and changes can only be pushed here from dev branch. You will not be able to push to main branch directly from feature branch as feature branch may contain untested / brittle code that may break the overall codebase.

docs.title: Quickstart commands in GitHub
docs.text:
To run these commands below, open powershell, type bash. It will open a new linux session on your powershell. you can then navigate to the git repository folder on your local machine and run the below commands.

Note: - Directories in linux start with /mnt/c/... for C drive etc. - In windows the directory is C:\System32, and in bash, it will be /mnt/c/System32 . So slashes are different in windows and bash - if you run git commands from a directory, which does not contain a git repo, it will throw an error

  • clone the repository for the first time to your local system:

git clone git@github.com:Public-Health-Wales/.git

  • switch to an existing branch

git checkout

  • create a new branch

git checkout -b

  • stage your changes

git add .

  • commit your changes to your local branch

git commit -m "your commit message goes here"

  • push to the remote version of your branch git push

  • push to the remote branch for first time (usually local and remote branches have same name)

git push --set-upstream origin

  • check the status of your local branch

git status

  • To sync your local repo with remote repo

git pull

docs.title: Clone repository: Detailed steps
docs.text:
1. Create a local folder (I used my OneDrive) with the project name e.g. PCC NDAP
  2. Right click and open GitBash in that folder
  3. Now in GitHub navigate to the repo, in the top RHS of the page there is a green '<> Code' button, click on this then click the copy icon next to the repo web url
  1. Back in GitBash type 'git clone' then right click and paste the url for your repo e.g. 'git clone https://github.com/Public-Health-Wales/ndap-app-rdd-pcc.git' If you do not specify a target directory then it will clone the repo in your current working directory
  1. Press enter & you should see the repo now appears in your local folder
  2. Remember to pull to update your repo

docs.title: Branching, commit, push & pull : Detailed steps
docs.text:
This guide takes you through the process of committing a change, making a pull request, merging changes, and pruning the feature branch.

  1. Ensure you have loaded the repo in VS code
  2. Bottom LHS click develop:

  1. Then click Create new branch from in top search bar options:

  1. Then click develop branch
  2. Then option to give it a name feature/NAME. For example: feature/holly-test-2 & Press enter You are now checked out and working on the new branch

  1. Now you can go ahead and edit your script and make your changes. I've made a very simple change to test it.

  1. Now click the file and then Save
  2. Go back to little branch icon which, has a 1 to show a change, to open up branches

  1. Now can see commit button and also you can click on your changes and view them side by side

  1. Add comment for your commit in the Message box Then click commit No staged changes - click Yes

  1. you can click the + icon by your change in the script and it then stages the change

  1. You might get this error message when you try to commit:

  1. In a cmd terminal you need to paste:
  2. git config user.name "YOUR NAME"
  3. git config user.email "YOUR WORK EMAIL" And it will be resolved

  1. Once you have committed the change you will see a change to the commit button will be greyed out.

  1. You can go and check in github that your commit has been pushed

  1. Now need to merge changes into develop or get them reviewed by a colleague and then merged This process is called a pull request.

  1. Click new pull request
  2. Typically you would merge into develop first
  3. Select base as develop and compare to your branch
  4. Now can see your changes in github
  5. Title is populated from your commit message
  6. Can add description
  7. Then click create pull request
  8. On RHS you can click the settings and add a reviewer for the pull request
  9. The reviewer will see the following screen:

Click Add your review 21. The you get the review screen - Check line by line - Can add in any comments needed 22. If you click the plus, you can add any comments or code suggestions 23. Once you have - added your comments/suggestions - You click Start a review - Then you you see this screen 24. Select one of the options to Comment/Approve/Request changes then click Submit review 25. Then the requestor will have a pull request to action 26. Then you can click Apply the suggestion and Commit changes If there was no suggestion then reviewer would just click Approve and then you would click Merge 27. Or you can use the Files changes tab & Click Apply suggestion 28. Reviewer can now approve the commit 29. Look at the pull request, you should see the following: 30. Click ready to merge on RHS, Then merge pull request 31. Sign it has merged: 32. If you want you can delete the branch: 33. Your local repo will be resynced when you do a git pull in VS code - Change branch back to develop (from your deleted feature branch) - Pull - You might need to manually delete it locally too

docs.title: A Guide to setup and work in VSCode
docs.text: This document lays out steps on how to setup VSCode and execute R code from VSCode

docs.title: VSCode: What is it?
docs.text:
Visual Studio Code is a code editor (produced by Microsoft) which can handle a number of different coding languages (R, python, markdown, HTML and CSS, java) - different to RStudio therefore which only handles R.

https://code.visualstudio.com/

VS Code also has Git commands built-in and a user-friendly interface for Git.

docs.title: How To Setup VSCode to run R files: Overview
docs.text:
This section is a overview steps required to run R files in VS Code:

  1. Install two extensions in VS Code (extensions are the VS Code equivalent of 'packages' in R);
  2. Install two packages in R: 'languageserver', 'httpgd'; install the packages into the library of the version of R that you want to use in VS Code.
  3. Install 'radian' in VS Code (via a terminal window in VS Code). Radian provides a modern R console that corrects many limitations of the official R terminal and supports many features such as syntax highlighting and auto-completion.
  4. Install pandoc for Windows (in order to run/knit R Markdown files; this can be done without admin permissions);
  5. Check which version of R is being picked up by VS Code - you may want to specify which version of R to use in VS Code (if you have more than one version of R installed on your system/profile).
  6. To specify which version of R to use in VS Code see the instructions here Changing R version in VS Code - Stack Overflow

docs.title: How To Setup VSCode to run R files: Detailed Steps
docs.text:
1. VS Code extensions: To install extensions in VS Code, navigate to the Extensions tab in the LH navigation menu, and search for the required extension. Then click on 'Install'.

  2. R Extension for Visual Studio Code - see background details

  3. R Debugger - to support R debugging capabilities
  4. Install radian – in a PowerShell terminal in VS Code, run the command pip install -U radian
  5. R packages:
  6. Open RStudio, and install the packages into the version of R that you want to use in VS Code. You can also install packages via an R terminal in VS Code.
  7. Install languageserver and httpd
  8. Install pandoc for Windows:
  9. pandoc install Go to this page, and click on the Download the latest installer for Windows (64-bit) button. You will probably get an IT alert about the filetype, but you have the option to click Progress to continue with the download. Run the installer file when it is downloaded.
  10. To check that VS Code can find the pandoc installation, open VS Code (or restart VC Code if you had it open whilst installing pandoc), open an R terminal, and run the command rmarkdown::find_pandoc()
  11. Check which version of R is being picked up by VS Code:

The default intro text will display the version of R being used. 6. To manually amend the path to the R version that you want to use, in VS Code, open Settings | Extensions, then scroll down to the options for the R extension. Add the path to the R.exe file into the [Rpath: Windows] box, and the path to the Rterm.exe file into the [Rterm: Windows] box.

docs.title: How to Edit & Add A Page: Data Engineers
docs.text: Welcome! This guide helps you get set up and start working with the NDAP Documentation platform.

docs.title: 👥 Who is this for?
docs.text:
• Data Engineers
  • Developers working with data pipelines or datasets

docs.title: 🎯 What you’ll achieve
docs.text:
By the end of this guide, you will:

  • Have access to the documentation repository
  • Be able to run docs locally
  • Understand how to contribute changes
  • Know where to go next

docs.title: ✅ Open VS Code in WSL
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code
  2. select clone git repository

docs.title: ✅ If not using WSL, open VS Code
docs.text:
1. Launch VS Code by double-clicking the desktop icon or searching for it in the Start Menu
  2. Open the integrated terminal via Terminal in the top menu bar, then New Terminal
  3. Ensure the terminal type is set to Command Prompt - click the dropdown arrow next to the + in the terminal panel if it defaults to PowerShell

docs.title: ✅ Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:Public-Health-Wales/ndap_central_doc_repo.git
cd ndap_central_doc_repo

docs.title: ✅ Create Virtual Environment
docs.text:
WSL:

python3 -m venv .venv

Windows CMD:

python -m venv .venv

docs.title: ✅ Activate the Environment
docs.text:
WSL:

source .venv/bin/activate

Windows CMD:

.venv\Scripts\activate

docs.title: ✅ Check if pip is working
docs.text:
python -m ensurepip --upgrade
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

docs.title: ✅ Install dependencies
docs.text: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: ✅ Check if local site is working
docs.text:
WSL:

mkdocs serve

Windows CMD:

python -m mkdocs serve

Then open your browser at: http://127.0.0.1:8000

docs.title: ✅ Create new branch
docs.text:
git checkout -b feature/your-branch-name

⚠️ Branch names cannot contain spaces, use hyphens.

docs.title: ✅ Edit Documents
docs.text: Every folder must have this structure: 1. .pages - all markdown pages must be listed here under the nav block 2. index.md - must be present. This is the landing page. Write an overview or anything else appropriate for your team's landing page. 3. any other file.md as needed 4. all files except .pages must be .md format

docs.title: ✅ Commit and push to git
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Update documentation"
git push origin feature/your-branch-name

docs.title: ✅ Merge to Main
docs.text:
1. Raise PR to Main
  2. Merge PR to main
  3. Once merged, GH Actions will trigger two pipelines
  4. Wait until the "Pages build and deployment" workflow is complete

docs.title: ✅ Check the updated site
docs.text: Navigate to: https://Public-Health-Wales.github.io/ndap_central_doc_repo/

docs.title: ✅ Troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. Please do not touch any other file apart from your team's folder
  2. Check if your files are correctly listed under the nav section in the .pages file in your folder
  3. Check if the local site is working before pushing to the live site
  4. If nothing is working, please reach out to the DE team
  5. pip not working:
python -m ensurepip --upgrade
  1. mkdocs not found:
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
  1. site not updating: check if the PR is merged and the Pages build & deployment Actions workflow is complete
  2. navigation issues: check if your .md files are listed under the nav section of the .pages file

docs.title: How To Edit A Page
docs.text:
Welcome! This guide shows you how to view and update documentation easily — no Git or local setup required.

👉 Found something outdated? Fix it in seconds using the steps below.

docs.title: 👥 Who is this for?
docs.text:
• Users who want to improve or update documentation
  • Anyone who prefers a simple, browser-based workflow
  • Anyone who is NOT looking to make any operational / visual / styling / technical changes to the site

docs.title: 🧠 Before you start
docs.text:
• ❌ You do NOT need to create branches manually
  • ❌ You do NOT need to install anything
  • ✅ Everything can be done in the browser
  • ✅ You write, we take care of the rest

docs.title: 🎯 What you’ll achieve
docs.text:
By the end of this guide, you will:

  • ✅ Know how to update documentation pages
  • ✅ Be able to submit changes without using Git commands
  • ✅ Understand how your changes go live

docs.title: ✏️ Go to the documentation site
docs.text: 👉 NDAP Knowledge Hub

docs.title: ✏️ Navigate to the page you want to edit
docs.text:
• Find the page you want to improve
  • Read through the content

docs.title: ✏️ Click “Edit this page”
docs.text:
• At the top/right of the page
  • This opens the page in GitHub

docs.title: ✏️ Make your changes
docs.text:
• Edit text directly in the browser
  • Use the Preview tab to check formatting

docs.title: ✏️ Submit your update
docs.text:
Scroll down and click "Commit changes" Keep the default option of 'Create a new branch...' You can ignore the commit description Click "Propose changes"

👉 This will:

  • Automatically create a branch ✅
  • Take you to a Pull Request (PR) creation page ✅
  • Create a pre-populated PR template for you to fill (optionally) ✅
  • Although filling the PR description is not mandatory, we strongly recommend you write at least a short description of changes you are making ✅

Press "Create PR" button

docs.title: ✏️ What happens next
docs.text: • Let us handle the rest while you go and have a cuppa ☕

docs.title: ✏️ Optional read: Behind the scenes
docs.text:
• Once you create the PR, github workflow triggers
  • It runs a strict validation check to ensure your changes are not breaking anything
  • It does a rebase i.e. it moves the head to to the top of main branch
  • Then it merges the current PR to the main branch
  • Once merge is successful, it deletes the current branch. If needed, it can be restored within 30 days.
  • After that, it builds the site and publishes through github pages

docs.title: ✅ Don’t worry about making mistakes
docs.text:
• Changes are reviewed before going live
  • If something needs fixing, we’ll help ✅

Just share what you know — even small improvements help!

docs.title: 💡 Tip
docs.text: You don’t need any Git or technical knowledge to contribute. Just click Edit on any page and make your changes—the system handles the rest ✨

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: This section answers common questions about using and editing the site.

docs.title: ❓ Do I need Git or technical knowledge to edit pages?
docs.text:
No.

✅ You can edit pages directly in the browser ✅ Just click Edit, make your changes, and commit

The system handles everything else automatically.

docs.title: ❓ How long does it take for changes to appear?
docs.text:
Most changes are published within:

✅ A few minutes ✅ Up to 5 minutes in some cases

To see your update: - Refresh the page (Ctrl + F5)

If you don’t see your update: - Refresh the page (Ctrl + Shift + R)

docs.title: ❓ What happens after I click “Commit changes”?
docs.text:
When you commit:

  1. A change request is created
  2. The system checks your update to make sure its not breaking anything
  3. It is merged and published automatically

You don’t need to do anything else.

docs.title: ❓ Why didn’t my changes get published?
docs.text:
This usually happens when:

  • Someone else edited the same page at the same time
  • The system couldn’t safely combine both updates

👉 See Common Issues for what to do next

docs.title: ❓ Can I edit someone else’s page?
docs.text:
Yes.

✅ This is a shared knowledge base ✅ Anyone can improve or update content

docs.title: ❓ Can I undo a change?
docs.text:
Yes.

  • You can edit the page again and correct it
  • Or revert changes using GitHub if needed

docs.title: ❓ How do I create a new page?
docs.text:
• Go to the repository
  • Click Add file → Create new file
  • Add your content
  • Update the .pages file to include it in navigation

👉 See How To Add A Page for detailed steps

docs.title: ❓ Why is my image not showing?
docs.text:
Common causes:

  • File not uploaded
  • Incorrect path
  • File name mismatch

👉 See Images and Files for guidance

docs.title: ❓ Why does my formatting look wrong?
docs.text:
Common causes:

  • Missing blank lines
  • Incorrect headings
  • List indentation issues

👉 See Formatting Guide for examples

docs.title: ❓ Where should I put images and files?
docs.text:
• Images → images/ folder
  • Documents (PDFs, etc.) → files/ folder

Keep things organised and easy to find.

docs.title: ❓ When should I create a new page vs edit an existing one?
Edit existing page if:
docs.text:
• The topic already exists
  • You are improving content

docs.title: Create a new page if:
docs.text:
• The topic is new
  • The content would make an existing page too long

docs.title: ❓ What if I make a mistake?
docs.text:
No problem ✅

  • You can edit the page again and fix it
  • All changes are tracked and can be corrected

docs.title: ❓ Who do I contact if I’m stuck?
docs.text:
If you can’t resolve your issue:

  • Check Common Issues first
  • Then contact the support team (see Who to Contact)

docs.title: 💡 Tip
docs.text: If something doesn’t work as expected, try again after refreshing or reapplying your changes. Most issues are temporary and resolve quickly.

docs.title: Who to Contact
docs.text: If you’re unable to resolve an issue or need additional support, use the options below.

docs.title: ✅ Before Reaching Out
docs.text:
Before contacting someone, please check:

  • Formatting Guide – for styling issues
  • Common Issues – for publishing or update problems
  • FAQ – for quick answers

Many issues can be resolved quickly using these pages.

docs.title: 💬 Primary Support Channel
docs.text:
For general help or questions:

  • Use your team’s shared communication channel (e.g. Teams / Slack)
  • Include:
  • Link to the page you were editing
  • A short description of the issue

This helps others assist you faster.

docs.title: 👥 Content Maintainers
docs.text:
If your issue relates to specific content:

  • Contact the team or person responsible for that area
  • This could be:
  • Data owners
  • Project leads
  • Subject matter experts

docs.title: ⚙️ Technical Issues
docs.text:
For issues such as:

  • Changes not publishing
  • Errors during editing
  • Broken site behaviour

Contact the platform or engineering team responsible for maintaining the site.

docs.title: 🚨 When to Escalate
docs.text:
Reach out if:

  • Your changes are not appearing after a few minutes
  • You see persistent errors
  • You are unsure how to resolve a conflict
  • Something appears broken or incorrect

docs.title: ✅ What to Include When Asking for Help
docs.text:
To get faster support, include:

  • Page link
  • What you were trying to do
  • What went wrong
  • (Optional) Screenshot

docs.title: 💡 Tip
docs.text: Most issues are quick to resolve. Providing clear details will help others assist you efficiently.

docs.title: Content Guidelines
docs.text:
This page explains how to write and organise content to keep the site clear, consistent, and easy to use.

You don’t need technical knowledge—just follow these simple rules.

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose of This Site
docs.text:
This site is a shared knowledge base.

✅ Anyone can contribute ✅ Content should be easy to read and understand ✅ Information should be accurate and up to date

docs.title: 🧱 Page Structure
docs.text: Every page should follow a simple structure:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Briefly explain what the page is about.

docs.title: Main Content
docs.text: Break into clear sections using headings.

docs.title: Example (optional)
docs.text: Add examples where useful.

docs.title: Notes (optional)
docs.text: Any additional useful information.

docs.title: ✅ Keep it simple
docs.text:
• Use plain language
  • Avoid jargon where possible

docs.title: ✅ Be clear and direct
docs.text:
• Write short sentences
  • Get to the point quickly

docs.title: ✅ Be consistent
docs.text:
• Use similar wording across pages
  • Follow existing patterns

docs.title: 📌 When to Create vs Edit a Page
✅ Edit an existing page if:
docs.text:
• The information already exists
  • You are improving or updating content

docs.title: ✅ Create a new page if:
docs.text:
• The topic is new
  • The content would make an existing page too long

docs.title: 🧭 Page Naming
docs.text:
Choose clear and descriptive titles.

✅ Good examples: - Data Access Guide - How to Request Access - Pipeline Overview

❌ Avoid: - Generic names like "Notes" or "Stuff" - Very long or unclear titles

docs.title: ✅ Use headings
docs.text: Break content into sections:

docs.title: ✅ Use lists
docs.text:
Instead of long paragraphs:

  • Step 1
  • Step 2
  • Step 3

docs.title: ✅ Keep sections short
docs.text:
• Avoid large blocks of text
  • Split content into smaller sections

docs.title: 👥 Audience Awareness
docs.text:
Write for your audience:

  • Analysts
  • Scientists
  • Engineers

✅ Assume basic knowledge ❌ Don’t assume deep technical expertise

docs.title: ✅ Link related pages
docs.text:
Help users navigate easily:

  • Link to relevant guides
  • Avoid duplication

docs.title: 🖼️ Images and Diagrams
docs.text:
Use visuals when helpful:

✅ Use images to explain complex steps ✅ Keep file names simple and descriptive ✅ Store images in the correct location

docs.title: 🔄 Updating Content
docs.text: ✅ Keep pages up to date ✅ Fix outdated or incorrect information ✅ Improve clarity when needed

docs.title: ⚠️ Avoid These Common Issues
docs.text: ❌ Very long paragraphs ❌ Duplicate content across pages ❌ Unclear or vague explanations ❌ Overly technical language ❌ Missing structure

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This page explains how to request access to a dataset.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Submit a request form
  2. Wait for approval
  3. Access the dataset

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Contact the data team if you have issues.

docs.title: ❌ Bad Example
docs.text:
• No headings
  • Long paragraph with no structure
  • Unclear instructions

docs.title: ✅ Quick Checklist Before Saving
docs.text:
• Is the title clear?
  • Is the content easy to read?
  • Are headings used properly?
  • Are there unnecessary duplicates?
  • Would someone new understand this?

docs.title: 💡 Tip
docs.text: If you’re unsure, keep it simple and follow the structure used in other pages. Consistency is more important than perfection.

docs.title: Formatting Guide
docs.text: This site uses Markdown for writing content. You don’t need any technical background—just follow these simple patterns.

docs.title: Page Title
docs.text: Use once per page

docs.title: Headings
docs.text: Use headings to organise your content clearly.

docs.title: Sub-section
docs.text: ✅ Use headings to break content into sections ❌ Don’t skip levels (e.g. jumping from # to ####)

docs.title: 📝 Paragraphs
docs.text:
Keep paragraphs short and readable.

This is a paragraph.

This is another paragraph.

✅ Always leave a blank line between paragraphs

docs.title: Bullet Lists
docs.text:
• Item one
  • Item two
  • Item three

docs.title: Numbered Lists
docs.text:
1. Step one
  2. Step two
  3. Step three

✅ Use lists instead of long paragraphs ✅ For detailed guidelines : How to add lists in markdown

docs.title: 💻 Code Blocks
docs.text:
Use code blocks to display commands or code clearly.

Example:

pip install mkdocs

(If using Markdown source, wrap with three backticks)

✅ Keeps formatting clean and readable

docs.title: 🔗 Links
docs.text:
Example external link:

https://example.com

Example internal link:

../index.md

✅ Use descriptive links where possible

docs.title: 🖼️ Images
docs.text:
Example:

../images/example.png

✅ Make sure: - Image file has been uploaded - Path is correct - File name matches exactly (case-sensitive)

docs.title: 📊 Tables
docs.text:
Name Role Alex Analyst Sam Engineer

✅ Keep tables simple and aligned ✅ For detailed guidelines: Adding tables in Markdown

docs.title: 💡 Notes, Tips & Warnings
docs.text:
You can highlight important information:

!!! note This is a note

!!! tip This is a useful tip

!!! warning This is a warning

✅ Use these for important or helpful information

docs.title: ✏️ Text Formatting
docs.text:
Bold text:

Bold text

Italic text:

Italic text

✅ Use bold for emphasis ✅ Use italics sparingly

docs.title: 🧠 Best Practices
docs.text: ✅ Keep content simple and readable ✅ Use headings to structure your content ✅ Break content into sections ✅ Prefer lists over long paragraphs ✅ Add examples where helpful

docs.title: ⚠️ Common Mistakes
docs.text: ❌ Missing blank lines ❌ Incorrect heading levels ❌ Broken image paths ❌ Large blocks of text without structure ❌ Incorrect list indentation

  2. Step two

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Any additional information.

docs.title: ❓ Need More Help?
docs.text:
If formatting still looks incorrect:

  • Check spacing and indentation
  • Compare with examples above
  • Refer to the Common Issues page

docs.title: Images and Files
docs.text: This guide explains how to add images and files to your pages so they display correctly on the site.

docs.title: Step 1: Upload the image
docs.text:
1. Go to the appropriate folder (e.g. docs/images/)
  2. Click Add file → Upload files
  3. Upload your image
  4. Click Commit changes

docs.title: Step 2: Add the image to your page
docs.text:
Use the relative path to reference the image:

../images/example.png

docs.title: ✅ Good Practices for Images
docs.text:
• Use clear and descriptive file names
  • Keep file names simple (no spaces if possible)
  • Use lowercase (recommended)
  • Store images in a dedicated folder (e.g. images/)

Example:

data-flow-diagram.png

docs.title: ❌ Image not showing
docs.text:
Possible causes: - File not uploaded - Incorrect path - File name mismatch (case-sensitive)

Fix: - Confirm the file exists in the repository - Check the path matches exactly - Ensure spelling and casing are correct

docs.title: Step 1: Upload the file
docs.text:
• Navigate to the correct folder (e.g. docs/files/)
  • Click Add file → Upload files
  • Upload your file
  • Click Commit changes

docs.title: Step 2: Link the file
docs.text:
Use the relative path:

../files/example.pdf

docs.title: ✅ Good Practices for Files
docs.text:
• Use clear file names
  • Organise files into folders (images/, files/, etc.)
  • Avoid duplicate files
  • Keep file sizes reasonable

docs.title: 🔗 Linking Files in Text
docs.text:
You can include files in your content like this:

Download the file here: ../files/example.pdf

docs.title: 🧠 Folder Structure Example
docs.text:
docs/

  • images/
  • diagram.png

  • chart.png

  • files/

  • guide.pdf
  • template.xlsx

docs.title: ✅ Quick Checklist
docs.text:
Before saving your page:

  • Is the file uploaded?
  • Is the path correct?
  • Does the file name match exactly?
  • Is the file placed in the right folder?

docs.title: 💡 Tip
docs.text: If something doesn’t display correctly, it’s usually due to the file path or file name. Double-check both before committing changes.

docs.title: Common Issues & Troubleshooting
docs.text: If something didn’t work as expected after you edited a page, you’ll likely find the answer here.

docs.title: My changes didn’t appear on the website
docs.text:
What’s happening After you click Commit changes, your update goes through an automated process: - A draft change is created - The system checks it - It is merged and published automatically

What to do - Wait 2-3 minutes and refresh the page - Try a hard refresh (Ctrl + Shift + R)

docs.title: I committed changes but nothing seems to happen
docs.text:
What’s happening Your change is being processed in the background. In some cases: - The system may be validating your update - The change may still be merging

What to do - Check the Pull Requests tab in GitHub (optional) - Wait till the PR status is Merged - Wait 2-3 minutes and refresh the page

docs.title: My changes didn’t get published
docs.text:
What’s happening Sometimes your change cannot be applied automatically. This usually happens when: - Someone else edited the same page at the same time - The system could not safely combine both updates - Your change broke something e.g. it has links to invalid pages etc.

What to do - Open your Pull Request (a link is shown after you commit) - You may see a message about a conflict - Re-apply your change based on the latest version of the page - You may see a message about validation failure - click on the red validation failure. - It will show you what failed - Close the PR, and correct it and re-commit.

👉 If unsure, contact the support team

docs.title: What is a “merge conflict”?
docs.text:
A merge conflict happens when: - Two people edit the same part of a page at the same time - The system cannot decide which version to keep

Example (simplified)

Two users edit the same sentence differently:

  • Person A: updates step instructions
  • Person B: rewrites the same section

The system cannot automatically combine them.

What the system does - It tries to automatically combine changes (most of the time this works ✅) - If not, it pauses and asks for manual resolution

What you should do - Open your edit again - Copy your changes - Apply them to the latest version of the page

docs.title: My formatting looks wrong
docs.text:
Common causes - Missing blank lines - Incorrect heading format - Improper list indentation

What to do - Check the Formatting Guide - Use simple Markdown formatting - Preview changes before committing

docs.title: My image is not showing
docs.text:
Common causes - Incorrect file path - Image not uploaded to the repository - File name mismatch (case-sensitive)

What to do - Confirm the image is uploaded - Check the file path - See the Images and Files Guide

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• You don’t need Git or coding knowledge
  • Most changes are published automatically within seconds
  • If something fails, it’s usually due to overlapping edits

docs.text:
If your issue isn’t listed here:

👉 Check the FAQ 👉 Or go to Who to Contact
